s: Zeus grants Sarpedon (a life lasting three generations of mortal men)
q: For wise Zeus ordained that he should live for three generations of mortal men and not waste away with old age.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Poseidon has child Bellerophon (with Eurynome)
q: So she lay in the arms of Poseidon and bare in the house of Glaucus blameless Bellerophon, surpassing all men in.... over the boundless sea.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Poseidon has child Neleus (with Tyro)
q: Tyro the daughter of Salmoneus, having two sons by Poseidon, Neleus and Pelias, married Cretheus, and had by him three sons, Aeson, Pheres and Amythaon.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Poseidon has child Pelias (with Tyro)
q: Tyro the daughter of Salmoneus, having two sons by Poseidon, Neleus and Pelias, married Cretheus, and had by him three sons, Aeson, Pheres and Amythaon.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Hesiod attributes parentage to Deucalion (in the first Catalogue)
q: That Deucalion was the son of Prometheus and Pronoea, Hesiod states in the first _Catalogue_, as also that Hellen was the son of Deucalion and Pyrrha.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Poseidon gives all manner of gifts
q: Happy he! For earth-shaking Poseidon gave him all manner of gifts.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Atalanta is a maiden (swift-footed and peerless in beauty)
q: Then straightway there rose up against him the trim-ankled maiden (Atalanta), peerless in beauty: a great throng stood round about her as she gazed fiercely, and wonder held all men as they looked upon her.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Atalanta has parent Schoeneus
q: fair Atalanta, swift of foot, the daughter of Schoeneus, who had the beaming eyes of the Graces

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Atalanta rejects marriage (despite being ripe for wedlock)
q: though she was ripe for wedlock rejected the company of her equals and sought to avoid marriage with men who eat bread.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Atalanta contends with Hippomenes (in a foot race for marriage)
q: Hippomenes seeks my coy-eyed daughter to wife; but let him now hear my wholesome speech. He shall not win her without contest

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Europa is mated with the Father of men and of gods (so far off)
q: when the Father of men and of gods had mated so far off with trim-ankled Europa

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Europa is carried to Crete (by Zeus in the form of a bull)
q: In this way he deceived Europa, carried her off and crossed the sea to Crete where he had intercourse with her.
